title: Laomedon. Hesione
source: P. Ovidius Naso, Metamorphoses, ed. Hugo Magnus (Gotha: F.A. Perthes), public domain; TEI from PerseusDL/canonical-latinLit phi0959.phi006.perseus-lat2, sha256 8719b7d375018d4f. Collated against The Latin Library (cltk mirror) as a disagreement detector only. Original spelling kept. Pronunciation convention: reconstructed Classical (restored) Latin, applied consistently. All translations were made fresh from the Latin for Lectorium.
about: Latona's son, his vengeance done, leaves Tmolus and comes down on Laomedon's fields, where an ancient altar to the Thunderer stands with the Sigean deep on one hand and the Rhoetean on the other. He finds the king first raising the walls of a new Troy, and together with the trident-bearing father of the swelling deep he puts on mortal shape and builds them for gold agreed in advance — which the king then denies, adding perjury to the broken bargain. The sea answers with a flood, and the king's daughter is demanded for a sea-monster; Alcides frees her, is refused the horses he was promised, and takes the twice-forsworn walls. Telamon comes away with Hesione, and the part closes on Peleus, whose goddess wife is set against a grandfather's name that more than one man can claim.

sentences.t:
Ultus abit Tmolo liquidumque per aera vectus
angustum citra pontum Nepheleidos Helles
Laomedonteis Latoius adstitit arvis.
sentences.l: Having taken his vengeance he goes away from Tmolus, and, carried through the liquid air, on this side of the narrow sea of Nephele's daughter Helle, Latona's son took his stand on Laomedon's fields.
sentences.i: His vengeance taken, he leaves Tmolus; and, borne through the clear air, Latona's son comes to a stand on Laomedon's fields, on the near side of the narrow sea of Helle, Nephele's daughter.
sentences.n: Ultus is the perfect participle of the deponent ulciscor, so it is active in force — “having taken vengeance”, not “having been avenged”. The subject is withheld: nothing names him until Latoius, “Latona's son”, in the third line of the unit. aera is the Greek accusative singular form of aer (Latin would be aerem), governed by per, and liquidum agrees with it; it is the plain object of the preposition, not an accusative of respect. citra, “on this side of”, stands between the adjective angustum and its noun pontum instead of before them. Nepheleidos Helles are Greek genitive forms, “of Helle, Nephele's daughter”; the narrow sea is the strait that carries her name. arvis has the ending shared by dative and ablative, and adsto normally takes the dative, “stood at” — which comes to the same thing here as the “on” of the translation.

sentences.t:
Dextera Sigei, Rhoetei laeva profundi
ara Panomphaeo vetus est sacrata Tonanti.
sentences.l: On the right of the Sigean, on the left of the Rhoetean deep, an old altar has been consecrated to the Panomphaean Thunderer.
sentences.i: With the Sigean deep on the right hand and the Rhoetean on the left, an ancient altar stands consecrated to the Thunderer Panomphaeus.
sentences.n: profundi, “of the deep”, is one genitive serving both Sigei and Rhoetei; Sigeum and Rhoeteum are the two promontories on this coast, and the adjectives here describe the water off each. dextera and laeva are ablatives of place with parte, “on the right side”, “on the left side”, left unexpressed. est sacrata is a perfect passive, “has been consecrated”, naming a state that still stands, and vetus, “old”, belongs to ara. Tonans, “the Thunderer”, is Jupiter; Panomphaeus is a cult title of his, built on Greek elements meaning roughly “of every oracular voice”.

sentences.t:
Inde novae primum moliri moenia Troiae
Laomedonta videt susceptaque magna labore
crescere difficili nec opes exposcere parvas
cumque tridentigero tumidi genitore profundi
mortalem induitur formam Phrygiaeque tyranno
aedificat muros, pactus pro moenibus aurum.
sentences.l: From there he sees Laomedon first raising the walls of a new Troy, and the great things undertaken growing by difficult labour and demanding no small resources; and together with the trident-bearing father of the swelling deep he puts on mortal shape and builds walls for the tyrant of Phrygia, having bargained for gold in return for the walls.
sentences.i: From there he sees Laomedon raising the walls of the new Troy for the first time, sees the great work taken in hand grow under hard labour and call for no small wealth; and, together with the trident-bearing father of the swelling deep, he puts on mortal shape and builds the tyrant of Phrygia his walls, with gold agreed as the price of them.
sentences.n: videt governs three accusative-and-infinitive clauses in a row: Laomedonta moliri, suscepta crescere, and exposcere with suscepta carried over as its subject. Laomedonta is the Greek accusative singular form of the name (Latin would be Laomedontem), the subject of the first infinitive. suscepta is a neuter plural participle used as a noun, “the things taken in hand”, the work in progress, and magna is neuter plural with it, “the great things taken in hand”: magna cannot belong to labore, which is masculine and would require magno. The ablative labore difficili is split across the line-end, labore closing 200 and difficili following the infinitive crescere in 201. nec ... parvas is litotes, “not small” for “very great”. In 202 the two adjective-noun pairs are interlocked — tridentigero belongs to genitore, tumidi to profundi — and the whole phrase describes the sea-god without naming him. induitur is a passive form used in the middle sense, “clothes himself in”, which is why it can take the direct object mortalem formam. pactus is the perfect participle of the deponent paciscor and so is active, “having struck a bargain”; it is singular and attaches to the one god who is the subject, though the building is shared. tyrannus is a Greek loanword for a sole ruler; in Latin verse it can name a king without in itself imputing blame, and this part's own next word for him, at 205, is rex. The walls are moenia at 199, then muros and moenibus within the single line 204; the two nouns are used of the same thing here.
Two words, and the imperfect stabat holds them still: the walls are up and standing. The colon is the archive's own punctuation, turning the finished work straight into what the king does with it.

sentences.t:
pretium rex infitiatur et addit,
perfidiae cumulum, falsis periuria verbis.
sentences.l: the king denies the payment and adds — the crowning heap of his treachery — perjuries with false words.
sentences.i: the king denies that the fee is owed and, to crown his treachery, adds perjury in lying words.
sentences.n: infitiatur is deponent, passive in form and active in sense, and means to disown a debt rather than simply to decline to pay it. perfidiae cumulum is an accusative in apposition to periuria: a cumulus is the heap piled on top of an already full measure, so the false oath is what is added to the broken bargain, not a separate offence beside it. falsis verbis is an ablative of means. periuria is plural where English wants a singular.

sentences.l: “You will not carry it off unpunished,”
sentences.n: feres is the future of fero, “carry, carry away”; with impune the phrase is the ordinary Latin threat to a wrongdoer, “you will not carry this off scot-free”. The threat comes before its speaker: the quoted words open the line and rector maris inquit, “says the ruler of the sea”, follows them in the same line.

sentences.t:
rector maris inquit et omnes
inclinavit aquas ad avarae litora Troiae,
inque freti formam terras complevit opesque
abstulit agricolis et fluctibus obruit agros.
sentences.l: says the ruler of the sea, and he tipped all his waters toward the shores of greedy Troy, and filled the lands into the shape of a strait, and took their wealth away from the farmers, and buried the fields under the waves.
sentences.i: said the ruler of the sea; and he tipped all his waters toward the shores of greedy Troy, flooded the land until it had the look of a strait, stripped the farmers of their wealth and buried their fields under the waves.
sentences.n: inquit is present where the verbs around it are perfect — inclinavit, complevit, abstulit — the speech kept in the present while the flood is told as done. obruit has the same form in the present and the perfect; the perfects beside it make the perfect the natural reading. avarae, “greedy”, is a genitive agreeing with Troiae: the epithet is fastened to the city itself, though it is the king who withheld the payment. in freti formam is “into the shape of a strait”: the drowned fields take on the look of open water. agricolis is a dative of separation with abstulit, “took away from the farmers”, and fluctibus an ablative of means with obruit.

sentences.t:
Poena neque haec satis est: regis quoque filia monstro
poscitur aequoreo;
sentences.l: Nor is this penalty enough: the king's daughter too is demanded for a monster of the sea;
sentences.i: And this punishment is not enough: the king's own daughter is demanded as well, for a beast of the sea;
sentences.n: neque is postponed behind poena, so the sentence opens on the word “penalty” and only then denies that it is sufficient. est is present, and the four verbs that carry the story from here to 215 — poscitur, vindicat, poscit, capit — are present with it, after the perfects that told the flood (inclinavit, complevit, abstulit); the part moves back and forth between the two tenses throughout, and recessit at 216 is perfect again. quoque here is the plain adverb “also”, not quo-que, “and by which”: there is no antecedent in the sentence for a relative. poscitur is passive with no agent expressed — these lines do not say who demands her. monstro aequoreo is the dative of the party she is demanded for.

sentences.t:
quam dura ad saxa revinctam
vindicat Alcides promissaque munera, dictos
poscit equos, tantique operis mercede negata
bis periura capit superatae moenia Troiae.
sentences.l: and her, bound fast to the hard rocks, Alcides sets free, and he demands the promised gifts, the horses that were named; and, the wage for so great a work having been refused, he takes the twice-forsworn walls of a conquered Troy.
sentences.i: and Alcides frees her from the hard rocks she is bound to, and demands the gifts he was promised, the horses named in the bargain; and when the wage for so great a work is refused, he takes the twice-forsworn walls of a beaten Troy.
sentences.n: quam is a connecting relative opening a new sentence — “and her” — with revinctam, “bound fast”, agreeing with it. Alcides is a patronymic, “descendant of Alceus”, and stands here in place of a name, as Latoius does at 196 and the trident-bearer at 202: this part names its heroes by their descent. promissa munera and dictos equos are one thing said twice: the promised gifts, and then the horses that were named as those gifts. mercede negata is a true ablative absolute, noun and participle standing free of the rest of the sentence, with tanti operis, “of so great a work”, depending on mercede. periura is a neuter plural adjective agreeing with moenia, so the walls carry the king's perjury; the “twice” counts the two broken bargains this part has shown, the gold denied at 205 and the horses denied now.

sentences.t:
Nec pars militiae, Telamon, sine honore recessit,
Hesioneque data potitur.
sentences.l: Nor did Telamon, a part of the campaign, withdraw without a reward, and he takes possession of Hesione, given to him.
sentences.i: Nor did Telamon, who had had his part in the campaign, come away unrewarded: Hesione is handed over, and he takes possession of her.
sentences.n: nec ... sine honore is a double negative, litotes for “with a good reward”; honos here is the prize paid for service, not abstract honour. militia is military service, or the force that renders it; pars militiae makes Telamon a share of the war rather than a man standing beside it. Telamon is the nominative subject in spite of the commas that flank it — recessit and potitur are both third person, so this is not an address to him — and pars militiae stands in apposition to the name. potior governs the ablative, so Hesione data is the verb's ablative complement, “gets possession of Hesione, given”, and not an ablative absolute, though it has the same shape. The Latin makes her the thing handed over, and does not stop over it.

sentences.t:
Nam coniuge Peleus
clarus erat diva:
sentences.l: For Peleus was famous by a wife who was a goddess:
sentences.i: For Peleus was distinguished by having a goddess for a wife:
sentences.n: coniuge ... diva is an ablative of cause with clarus, “made famous by”. Noun and adjective are pulled apart across the line-end: coniuge is the second-to-last word of 217 and diva the third word of 218, with Peleus, clarus and erat standing between them. Nam sets this beside Telamon's prize; these lines say nothing of how the two men are related.

sentences.t:
nec avi magis ille superbus
nomine, quam soceri, siquidem Iovis esse nepoti
contigit haud uni, coniunx dea contigit uni.
sentences.l: nor was he prouder of his grandfather's name than of his father-in-law's, seeing that to be Jupiter's grandson has fallen to not one man alone; a goddess as wife has fallen to one alone.
sentences.i: and he was no prouder of his grandfather's name than of his father-in-law's, since to be Jupiter's grandson has fallen to more than one man; a goddess for a wife has fallen to one man only.
sentences.n: superbus takes the ablative nomine, “proud in the name”, and the two genitives avi and soceri both hang on it, with nomine doing duty a second time for soceri. siquidem introduces the reason. contigit is used impersonally, with the infinitive clause as its subject and a dative of the person — “to be Jupiter's grandson fell to …”: haud uni is that dative, and nepoti is drawn into the dative to match it rather than standing as a nominative after esse. The closing line turns on repetition — contigit twice and uni twice, first denied and then affirmed. The father-in-law is not named here.
